content: 1. The enzyme CYP3A4 plays a critical role in the metabolism of many drugs. When co-administering capivasertib with moderate CYP3A inhibitors, the dose of capivasertib should be reduced, and therapy should be closely monitored. 2. Carbamazepine decreases the levels or effects of erythromycin stearate by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Conversely, erythromycin stearate increases the levels or effects of carbamazepine by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies should be considered due to the potential for serious interactions. 3. Erythromycin stearate reduces the efficacy of cefdinir, cefditoren, cefpodoxime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, and cefoxitin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Bacteriostatic agents like erythromycin may inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents. Close monitoring is recommended when these drugs are used concomitantly. 4. Cenobamate decreases the levels or effects of erythromycin stearate by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. When co-administered, the dose of CYP3A4 substrates may need to be increased. Therapy should be closely monitored. 5. Erythromycin stearate increases ceritinib levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of arrhythmias. Alternative therapies are recommended. 6. Erythromycin stearate increases the levels or effects of cevimeline by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 7. Chloroquine increases the toxicity of erythromycin stearate by prolonging the QTc interval. Caution is advised, and alternative therapies should be considered. 8. Chlorpromazine and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of arrhythmias. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 9. Erythromycin stearate reduces the efficacy of the cholera vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics, including erythromycin, may inactivate the vaccine strain. Cholera vaccine should not be administered to patients who have received antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 10. Erythromycin stearate increases cilostazol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose reduction of cilostazol to 50 mg twice daily should be considered. Alternative therapies are recommended. 11. Cimetidine increases erythromycin stearate levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 12. Erythromycin stearate increases cinacalcet levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 13. Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes in predisposed patients. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 14. Erythromycin stearate increases citalopram levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval, increasing the risk of arrhythmias. Alternative therapies are recommended. 15. Erythromycin stearate increases clarithromycin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and vice versa. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 16. Erythromycin stearate and clindamycin exhibit pharmacodynamic antagonism, potentially reducing each other's effects. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 17. Erythromycin stearate increases clomipramine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 18. Erythromycin stearate decreases clopidogrel activation by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, reducing its antiplatelet effect. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 19. Erythromycin stearate increases clozapine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 20. Erythromycin stearate and cobicistat both increase each other's levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 21. Erythromycin stearate increases cobimetinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If short-term use of moderate CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, the cobimetinib dose should be reduced to 20 mg daily. After discontinuation of the inhibitor, the cobimetinib dose should be resumed at 60 mg daily. 22. Erythromycin stearate increases colchicine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Co-administration is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. If necessary, the colchicine dose should be reduced as per prescribing information. 23. Erythromycin stearate increases conivaptan levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and vice versa. Co-administration is contraindicated. 24. Erythromycin stearate increases conjugated estrogen levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein. It may also decrease estrogen levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of estrogen, with a low risk of contraceptive failure. Alternative therapies are recommended. 25. Erythromycin stearate increases cortisone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein. Cortisone decreases erythromycin stearate levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 26. Crizotinib increases erythromycin stearate levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein. Erythromycin stearate also increases crizotinib levels. Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 27. Crofelemer increases erythromycin stearate levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Crofelemer minimally affects systemic CYP3A4 due to low absorption. Therapy should be modified and closely monitored. 28. Cyclophosphamide increases erythromycin stearate levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 29. Erythromycin stearate increases cyclosporine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein. Cyclosporine also increases erythromycin stearate levels. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 30. Erythromycin stearate increases dabigatran levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Co-administration should be avoided in patients with renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min for atrial fibrillation or <50 mL/min for DVT/PE treatment). 31. Dabrafenib decreases erythromycin stearate levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified and closely monitored. 32. Erythromycin stearate increases dactinomycin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 33. Erythromycin stearate increases dalteparin effects by decreasing its metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 34. Danazol increases erythromycin stearate levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 35. Danicopan increases erythromycin stearate levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Dose reduction of P-glycoprotein substrates may be necessary. Therapy should be closely monitored. 36. Erythromycin stearate increases dapsone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 37. Erythromycin stearate increases daridorexant levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. The daridorexant dose should not exceed 25 mg per night when co-administered with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. 38. Erythromycin stearate increases darifenacin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and vice versa. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 39. Erythromycin stearate increases darunavir levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and vice versa. Co-administration is contraindicated. 40. Dasatinib and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval. Erythromycin stearate also increases dasatinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, and vice versa. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 41. Erythromycin stearate increases daunorubicin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 42. Deferasirox decreases erythromycin stearate levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 43. Erythromycin stearate increases deflazacort levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein. The deflazacort dose should be reduced to one-third of the recommended dose when co-administered with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 44. Degarelix and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 45. Desflurane and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 46. Desipramine and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided, and alternative therapies are recommended. 47. Erythromycin stearate increases desloratadine levels by inhibiting its metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 48. Deutetrabenazine and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval. At the maximum recommended dose, deutetrabenazine does not prolong the QT interval to a clinically relevant extent. Caution and close monitoring are advised.
